raw_text:
The objective is to identify the reasons behind the variability in completion times across sites using the same nominal work process. This study aims to measure the measurable factors that contribute to these differences and to differentiate between competing explanations. It will focus on understanding the sources of variability and their relative importance.

Assumptions
The study assumes that observable factors outside the control of the nominal work process directly affect completion times. It also assumes that completion times are subject to the influence of human behavior and external conditions, which may not be captured by the nominal work process.

Research design
A mixed-methods research design will be employed. Quantitative data will be gathered through surveys and performance metrics on variability in completion times, while qualitative data will come from focused interviews with key stakeholders across the sites.

Data or evidence needed
1. Surveys distributed to workers, managers, and other stakeholders at multiple sites to collect data on reported completion times, perceived workload, task prioritization, and other relevant factors.
2. Performance metrics on the actual completion times of tasks, available from operational databases at each site.
3. Interview transcripts from selected stakeholders to gather insights into observed practices, resource allocation, and potential sources of variability.

Measurement
Measures will include:
- Completion time (as the primary outcome)
- Perceived workload
- Task prioritization
- Resource availability
- Stakeholder roles and responsibilities

Analysis
Quantitative data will be analyzed using multivariate statistical techniques to identify correlations and potential predictors of completion time variations. Qualitative data will be analyzed using thematic analysis to identify trends and patterns in stakeholder perceptions and behaviors.

Decision / stopping rule
The research will culminate in a model that predicts completion time based on measurable factors. The stopping rule will be reached when no further significant changes in the predictors’ impact on completion time are observed in the multivariate analysis and when themes in qualitative data confirm the findings from quantitative analysis.

Limitations
Potential limitations include the possibility of subjective reporting in surveys, variability in task complexity across sites, and the challenge of replicating findings in different organizational contexts. Additionally, the mixed-methods approach may introduce complexity in data integration, requiring careful synthesis and validation methods.
